$comment: Keyed, MadeOnSol, one request per candidate. A GATE, not a score: it asks whether a
deployer is competent, which is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. Stage 0 demonstrates
the gap empirically — it shows the gate PASSING the one deployer we know is not worth the
time.
ON THE VENDOR READING — the MadeOnSol profile leg, which is what --ownership-only runs and
feed.mjs grade on — the denominator is `profile.pump_tokens[].complete` and nothing else.
Never `bonding_rate`, `total_bonded`, `total_tokens_deployed`, `recent_bond_rate`,
`recent_outcomes` or `best_token_peak_mc`, which are trailing windows or stale; and never
/deployer-hunter/{wallet}/tokens, which is bonded-only and so has no denominator at all.
THAT SENTENCE IS SCOPED TO THAT LEG AND IS NOT WHAT THE GATE READS BY DEFAULT (captain
decision 238a narrows it rather than deleting it: it was written about the vendor leg, it
remains true of the vendor leg, and it was only ever unlabelled). screen.mjs gates on the
CREATION-DERIVED MERGED HISTORY, whose completion flags come from the chain's own
bonding-curve state (creation.mjs -> mergeHistories, counted as `bondedFromCurve`) for
launches the vendor page never lists, with the listing's own flag only as the fallback where
the curve went unread. `justification.minCompletionRate` names the reading each bar is
measured on and owns that distinction — read it before quoting this paragraph as the gate's
source.

justification.completionRateSource: NOT A THRESHOLD — the field the other three bars are computed from ON THE VENDOR READING, and the reasoning for it is this block's $comment at length: profile.pump_tokens[].complete agreed with our tape 67/67 on the completion flag with no in-window launch missing, while every published aggregate is a trailing ~7.5-day window their own alert text calls 'lifetime', and /deployer-hunter/{wallet}/tokens is bonded-only and so has no denominator at all. NAME THE LEG, THOUGH (captain decision 238a, which moves no value): that is the leg --ownership-only runs and feed.mjs grade on, and it is NOT screen.mjs's default. By default the three bars are computed over the creation-derived merged history instead, whose completion flags come from the chain's own bonding-curve state (creation.mjs -> mergeHistories, `bondedFromCurve`) for launches this field never lists — so this entry is the anchor for the vendor leg's denominator and not a statement that every gate reading uses it. `justification.minCompletionRate` names the reading each bar is measured on; `justification.minTokens` does the same for the count. Named here as well because this file's contract is that the anchor is in `justification`.
justification.minTokens: MadeOnSol's own spec tells consumers to gate on labeled_tokens >= 3. That is far too low: on our subject deployer a 22-token window read 0.6818 against a true 0.4310, so a window of ~22 was enough to be wrong by 58% relative. 25 is the floor at which their sliding-window artefact stops being the whole measurement, and it is 8x their published gate. NAME THE POPULATION, THOUGH: that evidence is about the VENDOR'S TRAILING WINDOW, while rank.mjs compares `completion.tokens` of whatever history reading the run produced — by default the creation-derived merged listing, which is larger and therefore easier to clear than the window this figure was measured on. The bar is a 'worth scoring at all' filter rather than a claim about the deployer, so the mismatch is bounded, but the two are not the same count and no measurement fixes 25 against the merged one. It is NOT enough for a lifetime claim, which is why the span is reported alongside and why long-horizon consistency is reported UNMEASURED.
justification.minCompletionRate: 0.25, HELD BY CAPTAIN DECISION 231a (2026-08-04), WHICH MOVES NO VALUE AND REWRITES THIS ENTRY: the defect was that the earlier text named NO READING, which made the number unauditable — a completion rate is not one quantity here and the two the tool computes differ by an order of magnitude on the same wallets. NAME THE READING FIRST. This bar is compared against the CREATION-DERIVED MERGED HISTORY that screen.mjs gates on by default — which mints the wallet CREATED, `historySource: "creation-derived"`, the default since record schema 4 with --ownership-only as the opt-out, and the reading of every candidate in the last real run (`runs/2026-08-04.json`, schema 12, 82 candidates, 82 of 82 creation-derived). That reading's median window on those candidates is 147.1 days and its median token count 1,386, and it is the WHOLE creation history for 57 of the 82 (`creation.wholeHistory`). THE VENDOR 70-RECORD PAGE IS A DIFFERENT AND SHORTER QUANTITY AND THIS BAR IS NOT MEASURED ON IT: median span 3.4 days on the same 82 wallets, page-capped at 70 records on 63 of them, and SUCCESS-BIASED rather than merely short, because ownership is a sellable position and the ones worth handing on are the winners — `yHCxHBEa…` shows 280 of the 749 mints it created and so reads 1.0000 on the page against 0.3071 on the gate reading. --ownership-only runs and feed.mjs read that page (FEED.md, 'Why the gate here reads ownership'), so the feed ledger's `completionRate` is not this quantity and a bar argued on one does not transfer to the other. WHAT FIXES THE VALUE, in order of weight. (1) THE CONTROL IS A HARD CEILING. `7ufmve7Z…` — the known-competent operator Stage 0 requires this gate to PASS — reads 0.4325 (109 of 252) on the gate reading, so ANY BAR ABOVE 0.4325 EXCLUDES A WALLET WE KNOW IS GOOD; and its own month-to-month rates span 0.256 (0.381, 0.354, 0.610, 0.375, 0.548, 0.429), so anything above ~0.35 puts it within one ordinary month of exclusion. Its committed-tape lifetime rate, 0.4310 over 239 launches and 103 bonded, is the same ceiling read off this repo's own primary record. (2) WHAT THE BAR DOES ON THE SCREEN'S OWN POPULATION, re-derivable offline from the committed record: over the 66 of that run's 82 candidates that clear minTokens and minSpanDays the median rate is 0.0187, 4 clear 0.25, only 2 clear 0.35, and 0.60 admits NOBODY — a bar that empties the run has spent the keyed allowance to produce no Stage 2 population at all. (3) THE REGIME ARTEFACT READS HIGHER THAN THE CONTROL ON THE VENDOR PAGE — AND THE ASYMMETRY REVERSES ON THE GATE READING, WHICH IS THE ONE THIS BAR IS COMPARED AGAINST. CAPTAIN DECISION 263b (2026-08-05) CORRECTS THIS ENTRY AND MOVES NO VALUE; the defect it fixes is that the earlier text quoted the artefacts on the VENDOR PAGE and the control on BOTH readings inside one sentence, then drew a conclusion that is true of neither reading on its own. TAKE THEM APART. ON THE VENDOR 70-RECORD PAGE the two wallets whose rates are a post-break short-window artefact read 1.0000 (`yHCxHBEa…`, old-regime record 0.1369) and 0.9429 (`GeBJSHK4…`, old-regime record 0.0462) against the control's 0.5429, so on that page there is indeed no bar that removes the two and keeps the control, and raising a bar measured THERE would remove the operator and keep the artefacts. ON THE GATE READING the same three wallets read 0.3089, 0.3303 and 0.4325, so THE ORDER INVERTS AND A BAR IN (0.3303, 0.4325] WOULD REMOVE BOTH ARTEFACTS AND KEEP THE CONTROL (`runs/2026-08-05-seed-comparison.md`, which measured all three the same day; the artefact gate readings are its contribution, the control's 0.4325 is §6 of `slot-zero-gate-bar-measure-own-population`, held in firstmate's records and not in this repo). THE MECHANISM IS THE DENOMINATOR, which is why the inversion is not a fluke of two wallets: the artefacts' page readings are computed over 70 records of a 751-creation and a 327-creation history, and the creation-derived denominator is what collapses 1.0000 to 0.3089. WHAT THAT DOES AND DOES NOT LICENSE. It does not move this bar and 263b explicitly does not: the evidence is n = 2 ARTEFACTS AND ONE CONTROL, ON ONE DAY, with the control's figure taken from one leg and the artefacts' from another about an hour apart; and a band whose lower edge is 0.3303 sits 0.1022 below a control whose own month-to-month rates span 0.256 — so an ordinary month for `7ufmve7Z…` could put it inside the band the artefacts were supposed to occupy, and the separation would vanish with nothing in a run saying so. It is recorded here because 231a's rule is that a bar names the reading it is measured on, and the old sentence's claim ('there is no bar') was a claim about the wrong reading; leaving that uncorrected while the finding existed is the same defect one level in. WHAT WOULD JUSTIFY ACTING ON IT: the same three-way comparison over enough artefacts and controls to say whether the inversion is a property of the readings or of these two wallets, plus a re-read across months rather than on one day. Until then what distinguishes an artefact from an operator is window length and reading, not rate, so the instrument remains an evidence-window rule or the reading itself — and this bar stays at 0.25. (4) THE ASYMMETRY THAT DECIDES WHERE IN THE 0.25–0.35 BAND TO SIT, and it points DOWN. A false REJECTION here is permanent and invisible: the wallet is graded, filed in feed/ledger.json and never offered again (ledger.mjs; the feed never re-polls a wallet already graded). A false ACCEPTANCE is visible and cheap: it costs Stage 2 keyless requests and is then refused by stage2_entry.minRoomLeft — which is exactly what Stage 0 demonstrates on every run, passing `7ufmve7Z…` on this gate and refusing it on room. This gate is 'necessary and nowhere near sufficient' (this block's $comment), so it is deliberately set to fail towards acceptance. 0.25 is also MadeOnSol's own published 'good'-tier bar, which is where the number came from; it is not what holds it now. PROVENANCE, AND IT IS SPLIT BECAUSE THE TWO HALVES ARE AUDITED DIFFERENTLY. FROM THE COMMITTED `runs/2026-08-04.json`, re-derivable offline with no vendor call: the 82-candidate figures (82 of 82 creation-derived, median gate-reading window 147.1 days, median 1,386 tokens, whole creation history on 57 of 82, vendor median span 3.4 days, vendor page capped at 70 records on 63 of 82), the 66-candidate sweep (median 0.0187, 4 clear 0.25, 2 clear 0.35, none clears 0.60), and `yHCxHBEa…`'s page-against-gate pair (1.0000 on the vendor page against 0.3071 on the gate reading, 280 of the 749 mints its ownership listing shows). FROM `slot-zero-gate-bar-measure-own-population` (held in firstmate's records, not in this repo), because these do NOT reproduce from that run record: the control `7ufmve7Z…`'s 0.4325 gate reading, its 0.5429 vendor-page reading and its 0.256 month-to-month range are §6; `GeBJSHK4…`'s 0.9429 is §4.2's live re-read of 2026-08-05, and its §0 summary quotes the same figure; the old-regime records 0.1369 (`yHCxHBEa…`) and 0.0462 (`GeBJSHK4…`) are §0 and §4.2; and the argument itself — the ceiling, the sweep's reading, the artefact comparison and the asymmetry — is §6, §6b, §7 and §8. AND THE VENDOR 70-RECORD PAGE SLIDES, so two snapshots of one wallet days apart legitimately differ and neither is stale: `GeBJSHK4…` reads 0.9429 on that 2026-08-05 re-read and 0.957143 in this repo's own committed `runs/2026-07-29-elite.json` and `feed/ledger.json`, one launch apart on a 70-record window — that gap is a property of the surface, and it is itself part of why this bar is measured on the creation-derived reading rather than on the page. That report's §8 recommends the 0.25–0.35 band and does not choose within it; 231a chooses 0.25 and changes nothing about what the screen admits. ONE CORRECTION TO IT MADE HERE RATHER THAN INHERITED: it dates the creation-derived default to 'schema 12', which is the SCHEMA OF THE RUN IT MEASURED — the default arrived at record schema 4.
justification.minSpanDays: A high rate earned inside a single day is a burst, not a record — and this bar measures exactly that: rank.mjs compares `completion.spanDays`, which is FIRST DEPLOY TO LAST DEPLOY over the gate's history reading, not time-to-bond. The two are not the same quantity and an earlier version of this entry justified the first with a distribution of the second, computed from `curve_last_tx_s`; that column is formally ruled a valid upper BOUND and not a usable timing (data/population-tape-2026-07-29/IMPORT.md, Corrections 4, median overshoot 8.85x), so the clause is withdrawn rather than re-derived and the column is not quoted here. The measured median graduation time on this operator is 1,042 s = 17.4 MINUTES (IMPORT.md, Corrections 5), so 14 days is orders of magnitude above what a launch needs to resolve: this bar exists to refuse a wallet whose whole history is one burst, not to wait for bonding. NOTE THE RESIDUAL GAP, which no span bar closes: a wallet that deploys most of its tokens in the last 48 hours of a 14-day span still clears this, and its unresolved launches then depress its completion rate — which errs towards rejection, the direction this tool prefers to fail in.

$comment: THE CANDIDATE DISCOVERY FEED — tools/deployer-screen/feed.mjs, documented in FEED.md.
A scheduled lane that surfaces deployers this project has NOT seen before, triages them on
the Stage 1 gate, and queues the survivors for the beatability screen. It supersedes the
re-open monitor (captain, 2026-08-02: a competent dev that tightened its own launch bot does
not loosen it again, so re-polling wallets already graded closed watches the one place a
window will not reopen; the opportunity is in the POPULATION, not the graveyard).
THESE BOUNDS EXIST BECAUSE THIS LANE RUNS FOREVER. Every other caller of the MadeOnSol key
is a one-off a human decided to spend. A scheduled lane is not, so an unbounded provider
call here is worse than anywhere else in the tool: a cron that drains the allowance leaves
the screen nothing. The feed's per-run keyed cost is 6 enumeration + at most gateBatch
profile requests — 6 and not 3 since captain decision 262a made the seeding TIERED by
default, one pass of all three endpoints per tier for `good` and `elite` (seed.mjs ->
DEFAULT_TIERS) — and NOTHING else in this lane is keyed.
THE DAILY ARITHMETIC, RESTATED AGAINST A DENOMINATOR THAT MOVED BY 500x (captain decision
267a, 2026-08-05): maxKeyedRequestsPerRun 18 x runsPerDayAssumed 6 = 108 worst case, of a day
that is now 100,000 requests and EXCLUSIVE to slot-zero rather than ~200 shared. At the
DEFAULT gateBatch of 6 it is 12 x 6 = 72. So this lane's worst case is 0.108% of the day where
it was 45% of it, and screen.mjs is left >=99,892 requests rather than >=110.
THE BOUNDS ARE KEPT ANYWAY, AND THAT IS THE POINT RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. The argument for
bounding a forever-lane was never only the size of the allowance: it is that a scheduled
consumer must state its cost in advance and be refused when it exceeds it, because a cron is
the one caller no human reviews before each spend. An unbounded lane against a 100,000-request
day is still an unbounded lane. So the ceiling MOVED ONLY WHERE THE TIERED PLAN FORCED IT
(15 -> 18, since 6 + maxGateBatch 12 = 18) and nowhere else — the upgrade bought no widening.
Raising runsPerDayAssumed without lowering the per-run ceiling is still how this lane silently
becomes the allowance's largest consumer — change both or neither.
THE FEED SPENDS NO KEYLESS REQUEST AT ALL. It grades on the ownership reading, which is one
keyed profile call, and does NOT walk the creation-derived history: that walk is ~100 RPC
requests per candidate at 2.5s apart, which no schedule can carry. The consequence is stated
rather than hidden — the ownership reading is biased in BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE (FEED.md, 'It
is biased in BOTH directions at once'): it REJECTS through the count bars and INFLATES through
the rate, so a feed failure is recorded as `held`, never as a rejection, AND a wallet that
clears it is not pre-validated either. The standing count of held wallets is printed by every
run. screen.mjs remains the authority.

justification.gateBatch: Six new wallets a run, six runs a day, is 36 gate readings a day for 72 keyed requests (it was 54 while enumeration cost 3; captain decision 262a's tiered default makes enumeration 6, so a default run costs 6 + 6 = 12). The two committed screen runs surfaced 22 and 72 distinct wallets from one enumeration each — runs/2026-07-29-elite.json and runs/2026-08-02-good.json, field coverage.distinctWalletsSeeded, from 74 and 150 rows returned — so a first live run defers most of what it sees and drains the backlog over the following days, which is why nextGateBatch is FIFO. An earlier version of this entry said 61 and 84; neither figure appears in either record (61 is feed/ledger.json's standing `held` count, a different quantity over the union of both runs), and the argument holds at 72 as it did at 84. Lower it if the screen needs more of the allowance; it can only ever be lowered from the command line.
justification.maxGateBatch: The hard cap --gate cannot exceed. 12 keeps the worst-case per-run keyed cost at 18 and therefore the assumed daily cost at 108. UNMOVED BY THE ULTRA UPGRADE, DELIBERATELY: 12 was chosen when 108 would have been over half a 200-request day, and against 100,000 exclusive it is 0.108%, so the number now bounds WALLETS GRADED PER RUN rather than a share of an allowance. It stays at 12 because how many strangers a cron grades unreviewed is a question about the LEDGER — a graded wallet is filed and never offered again (ledger.mjs), so a wrong gate reading taken at speed is permanent and invisible — and not a question about quota. A bound a flag can widen is not a bound.
justification.maxKeyedRequestsPerRun: 6 enumeration + maxGateBatch 12 = 18. It was 15 at 3 enumeration requests and HAD to move with captain decision 262a's tiered default, or every feed run would be refused before its first request at 6 + 12 = 18 > 15 — the same forced half budget.maxKeyedRequests has. Enforced before the first request: a plan whose worst case does not fit is refused with nothing spent, exactly as screen.mjs refuses one. NOTE WHERE THIS DIFFERS FROM budget.maxKeyedRequests, deliberately: that one is DOUBLED to cover the one-retry rule, and this one is not. The feed's client is constructed with maxRequests = this value and retries count against it (client.mjs, maxRetriesPerRequest default 1), so a retry-heavy feed run can be stopped mid-flight where a screen run cannot. That is the safer direction for a lane whose failure mode is a partially written ledger, and planFeedRun's refusal names the lever (--gate).
justification.runsPerDayAssumed: NOT enforced by the tool — nothing here can see a cron table. It is the number the daily arithmetic above is computed against, and it is recorded so that a schedule which contradicts it is contradicting a written figure rather than an assumption. Six runs a day is four-hourly.
justification.seedLimit: The page size asked of each enumeration query. 50 is the maximum recent-bonds and leaderboard accept (their spec's 100 returns HTTP 400) and is what alerts is clamped to as well, so this is 'as much as the vendor will give for one request' rather than a tunable.
justification.dryStreakAlarm: Three consecutive live, completed runs with no new wallet — an aborted run surfaced nothing because it stopped, so it is skipped rather than counted. One dry run is ordinary: the vendor's pages overlap heavily between runs and at four-hourly cadence most of what comes back is yesterday's list. Three in a row is saturation of what this vendor exposes, and it exits non-zero so a scheduler notices. A dead feed that reads as a healthy quiet one is the exact failure this lane was told to make impossible.
justification.runHistoryKept: 60 run rows, i.e. ten days at the assumed cadence. Enough to see a yield trend and to compute the dry streak; bounded so a committed ledger does not grow without limit.

$comment: The captain's word was 'consistently'. MadeOnSol cannot answer it: their only
denominator-complete surface (profile.pump_tokens) is capped at 70 records and about 35 days.
Manufacturing a long-horizon claim from a 35-day window is exactly the defect we found in
their own aggregate, so the tool does not do it. Long-horizon consistency is reported as
UNMEASURED unless --consistency is passed, which pages a keyless pump.fun creator listing and
spends no quota.

justification.default: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch. Long-horizon consistency is UNMEASURED unless asked for, because the only denominator-complete vendor surface is a ~35-day window and manufacturing a lifetime claim from it is the defect this tool exists to refuse. See this block's $comment.
justification.optIn: NOT A MEASUREMENT — the flag that turns the pass on. It pages a keyless pump.fun creator listing and spends no vendor quota.
justification.minEpochs: AN UNMEASURED OPERATIONAL BOUND, stated as one. What the code computes is max(epoch rate) - min(epoch rate) across qualifying epochs (rank.mjs), and a spread over 2 points is just the two ends: 3 is the smallest count at which 'spread' describes a distribution rather than a difference. That is arithmetic about the statistic, not evidence about deployers — nothing in this repo measures how many 30-day epochs a completion rate needs to stabilise. What would justify a specific value: bucket the subject's own 239 committed launches into 30-day epochs and show at what epoch count the dispersion figure itself stops moving. That is computable offline from data/population-tape-2026-07-29/launches.csv today and has not been run. Until it is, this is a floor chosen for the shape of the statistic, and the consequence of being wrong is bounded — consistency FLAGS and never filters (see maxDispersion), and below this floor the tool reports UNMEASURED rather than estimating.
justification.minTokensPerEpoch: AN UNMEASURED OPERATIONAL BOUND, and the same arithmetic minFieldRoundTrips makes explicitly: a rate over n tokens moves by 1/n when one outcome changes, so at 12 a single bond or failure moves an epoch's rate by 8.3 points and a bucket thinner than that is noise wearing a percentage sign. 12 is chosen for that property, not measured — no committed measurement says a 30-day epoch of a real deployer needs 12 tokens to be readable, and the vendor's own profile cap (70 records over ~35 days) is the reason most candidates will have few qualifying epochs at all. The same offline bucketing of launches.csv proposed for minEpochs would justify or move it. A bucket below the floor does not qualify, so the failure direction is UNMEASURED rather than a wrong rate.
justification.epochDays: 30-day epochs are long enough that an epoch is not one week of luck, and short enough that a 6-month history yields the 3 required.
justification.maxDispersion: max(epoch rate) - min(epoch rate) > 0.35 FLAGS a deployer as streaky rather than excluding it. A flag, not a filter: the point of the exercise is that one hot window must not read as a record, and the reader is entitled to see the spread rather than have it silently applied.

$comment: Bounds for the creation-derived launch history — the walk that answers 'which tokens did this
wallet CREATE' instead of 'which tokens does it OWN NOW'. See creation.mjs for why the two
differ and for the on-chain observation that established it.
This walk is the expensive part of a run by an order of magnitude, because the only keyless
index that reaches a create transaction is the wallet's own signature index, and for a pump.fun
deployer that index is dominated by strangers' failed trades. Every bound here is therefore a
hard ceiling, and readCreatedHistory reports which one bit rather than truncating silently.
The walk covers a CONTIGUOUS WINDOW BACKWARDS FROM NOW. Inside it every creation is found;
outside it none is, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing and says so. A
create count read as a lifetime figure under any stopReason other than 'index-exhausted' is
wrong in the same direction as the vendor's sliding 'lifetime' window.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: Measured 2026-08-02: sustained keyless throughput against api.mainnet-beta is about 0.42 transactions/second, i.e. roughly one request per 2.4s including backoff, and a create is found by inspecting every SUCCEEDED signature in the wallet's index. The success fraction varies enormously between deployers — 1.7% on the busiest wallet screened, 99.7% on another — so the cost of a full history ranged from 7 minutes to 84 hours across the 12 wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json. 100 requests is a per-candidate ceiling that keeps a 12-candidate run inside about 50 minutes; on a quiet wallet it is the whole history, on a busy one it is a window of hours and the record says so. NOTE THE OTHER END OF THAT ARITHMETIC: at the 195-candidate cap it is 19,500 requests and ~13.5 HOURS, which is the dominant cost of a default run — --candidates N is the lever that bounds it, and --ownership-only skips it for a fast pass whose bias is stamped into the record. See CREATION-DERIVED.md for the per-wallet costs.
justification.maxSignaturePages: 200 pages is 200,000 signatures, past which no keyless walk is finishing inside a session. It exists so a wallet with an enormous index cannot turn the request ceiling into the only brake.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, and there is no measurement behind the number. pumpfun.mjs stops the walk at transactionsInspected >= this, but a transaction is inspected one getTransaction at a time (txBatchSize 1) from a client capped at maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate 100, so AT MOST ~100 transactions can ever be inspected for one candidate — 8000 is unreachable by a factor of ~80, and every real walk stops on 'request-ceiling' or 'index-exhausted' instead. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising the request ceiling does not silently remove the only bound on inspection work, and it is documented as unjustified rather than given a manufactured anchor: what would justify a value is a measured cost per inspected transaction against a wall-clock budget, which only exists for the REQUEST ceiling (see maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate, 0.42 tx/s measured 2026-08-02). Delete it or re-derive it if the request ceiling ever rises above it.
justification.txBatchSize: 1, and the 1 is measured. report.md 9.4 recorded batches of 5-8 getTransaction as sustainable, and that no longer holds: on 2026-08-02, fetching the same transactions at batch=1 took 58s with ZERO load-shed events, batch=4 took 76s with 7, and batch=8 took 110s with 11. Throughput was 0.42 tx/s at batch=1 and 0.36 tx/s at batch=8 — the endpoint weights each entry of a JSON-RPC batch against its limiter, so a batch of 8 spends 8 tokens and buys nothing but backoff. Batching is therefore actively harmful HERE TOO, exactly as it is on pump.fun's keyless endpoints. The client still supports batching, capped at 8, because the endpoint's behaviour is the vendor's to change and re-measuring is cheaper than rebuilding.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: 1,400ms is the documented floor, but a 200-request run at that pace on 2026-08-02 took over 890 seconds instead of the expected 280 — the endpoint was shedding load and the retry backoff was paying for it. 2,500ms is the observed rate at which that stops happening, so it is faster in wall-clock than the nominally quicker setting. api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction, and two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout, so this is one queue with one request in flight.

$comment: CREATION ENUMERATION, PRIMARY SURFACE. Captain decision 156a, 2026-08-03. The same question
creation_walk and creation_walk_helius answer — 'which mints did this wallet CREATE' — read
off Dune's decoded pump.fun creation events instead of walked out of a signature index.
tools/deployer-screen/dune.mjs owns the method; CREATION-DERIVED.md section 8 owns the
reproduction and the measured cost.
THE SURFACE IS A UNION AND THE UNION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: pump_evt_createevent UNION
pump_call_create, deduped by mint. pump_call_create ALONE returns ZERO rows for our subject
(it decodes only the original Create; this deployer uses CreateV2). pump_call_create_v2 ALONE
is not backfilled before ~2026-04-28 and silently misses 101 of our 239 launches, `maxxing`
included. Attribution keys on "user"/account_user, the SIGNER — never on `creator`, which is
a settable CreateV2 argument that six bot-signed mints use to name our subject, inflating the
EVERY DUNE-DERIVED COUNT SHIPS WITH ITS OWN COVERAGE PROBE, and that is the binding condition
of the decision rather than a nicety. Decoded tables have SILENT START DATES: they return a
confident, well-formed, complete-looking answer that is simply wrong before their first row,
with nothing in the response saying so. Same failure shape as a truncated backwards walk in
pumpfun.mjs and the same direction: plausible and silent. dune.mjs -> assessCoverage refuses
a reading that reaches outside the probe, and a refused reading FALLS BACK to the walk — it is
never published as a measured count.
SPEND. Free tier, 2,500 credits/month, SHARED with whatever else holds the key. What a run
may spend against that allowance is CHECKED BEFORE ITS FIRST REQUEST — dune.mjs ->
checkDuneAllowance, and README.md -> 'The monthly credit ceiling' owns it — but nothing here
carries state ACROSS runs, so the arithmetic between them is still the operator's.
A FAILED EXECUTION IS STILL BILLED AND IS TERMINAL: client.mjs -> DuneClient never retries
one, and no code may wrap a retry around it. Budget from BILLED credits, not
execution_cost_credits, which understates by ~3.5x because retrieving results is ~71% of the
bill at ~20 credits/MB.

justification.creationQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved query the enumeration executes, pinned so a run names the surface it read. dune.mjs -> CREATION_SQL holds that query's SQL byte for byte and assertSavedQueryMatches compares the two BEFORE spending an execution, so a saved query edited from a browser fails the run loudly instead of returning a different measurement under the same name. Reused rather than created: it is the query `slot-zero-dune-evaluate` section 7 (held in firstmate's records, not in this repo) designates as the production shape, upgraded in place from event-only to the union, because the free tier allows only 10 private queries and the account holds 10. THEREFORE EVERY CHANGE TO CREATION_SQL IS A DEPLOY STEP AGAINST THIS QUERY ID: saved query 8204672 must be edited in place to the committed text before the next real run, because the comparison happens BEFORE the execution and a mismatch is not a wrong answer — it is a terminal refusal of the whole Dune leg on every run until they agree. There is no new query slot to create. tools/deployer-screen/README.md -> 'Deploying a change to the committed SQL' owns the step.
justification.coverageQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved coverage probe, pinned for the same reason and verified the same way against COVERAGE_SQL. It is the scout's own coverage query (report.md section 2) widened to carry min/max block time beside the monthly counts. It probes THREE tables while the enumeration reads TWO: pump_call_create_v2 is included precisely so the probe's own output demonstrates the boundary that disqualifies it, rather than this file asserting it in prose.
justification.maxExecutionsPerRun: 2, and the 2 is the exact plan rather than a round number: one execution for the enumeration, and at most one more to re-execute the coverage probe when the cached one has gone stale. Nothing else in a run may execute. An execution is BILLED WHETHER OR NOT IT SUCCEEDS and is never retried, so this is the bound on the only unrecoverable spend the Dune leg has. MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this account: the enumeration of 5 wallets / 482 rows cost 0.919 execution credits and 1.919 billed; the coverage probe cost 0.751 execution credits and 0.751 billed. AT THE 195-CANDIDATE CAP the execution cost barely moves — scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter, measured at 5 and at 20 — and what scales is bytes returned, which maxResultRows bounds. THIS BOUNDS ONE RUN, and it is what the monthly credit guard prices that run against: worstCaseCreditsPerExecution x this value is the compute half of the plan checkDuneAllowance compares with the account's remaining balance before the first request. The tool is still stateless BETWEEN runs, so the arithmetic across them stays the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxRequestsPerRun: Requests bound the WALL CLOCK and the polite use of a shared host; maxExecutionsPerRun bounds the money, and the two are separate ceilings because a poll loop that spent an execution's worth of budget on status checks would be counting the wrong thing. The arithmetic: each of the two possible executions costs 1 SQL-verification GET + 1 execute + up to maxPollAttempts 40 status polls + 1 results read = 43, so 2 x 43 = 86, plus the credit guard's single POST /usage and its one retry = 88, and the remaining 12 are the retry headroom (every read is retried at most once, and each attempt counts). 100 covers that sum. MEASURED: both executions on 2026-08-03 completed in 6-9 s, i.e. 2-3 polls, so a real run spends about 8 requests and the ceiling is a backstop rather than a budget.
justification.maxResultRows: 40,000 rows, RAISED FROM 20,000 BY CAPTAIN DECISION 264a (2026-08-05) AFTER THE CEILING REFUSED A REAL RUN, and THE UNIT THAT MATTERS IS STILL BYTES rather than rows, because results are billed at ~20 credits/MB and that is ~71% of the bill. WHAT LEAVING IT AT 20,000 COST, which is the whole evidence for the raise: 2026-08-05, an untiered default run at 76 deployers (runs/2026-08-05-seed-comparison.md, leg A). The per-deployer cap of 500 permitted 38,000 rows, the batch returned 27,731, and the reading was refused WHOLE — dune.rowsReturned 0, dune.coverage null, enumerationSource 'helius' on all 76 candidates. That leg then spent 232,937 Helius credits and 4,105 RPC requests against 1,924 and 33 for the 69-deployer leg that KEPT its Dune answer, i.e. ~121x the credits for the same measurement; and it lost captain decision 227a's mayhem flag entirely, mayhemShare null on 76 of 76, which means UNMEASURED and never 0%, since that flag is a Dune column no walk-sourced leg can report. The refusal itself was CORRECT — an unbounded read is an unbounded bill — so what was wrong is the ceiling, not the reader. TWO BOUNDS HOLD AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT BOUNDS. (1) THE BYTES BOUND, unchanged in method and re-priced: every result read is issued with `?limit=maxResultRows`, so no read can return more rows than this whatever the query does. `?limit=40000` was VERIFIED ACCEPTED by the vendor before this value moved (HTTP 200 against the production coverage query 8204603, 2026-08-05) rather than assumed to be in range. MEASURED 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns: ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes), and RE-MEASURED 2026-08-05 at the SIX columns CREATION_SQL selects today — `launches_total`, which makes the per-deployer cap below detectable instead of silent, and `is_mayhem_mode`, captain decision 227a's recorded-and-reported flag. The six-column shape reads 105.92 bytes/row batch-shaped (51,691 bytes over 488 rows, five wallets) and 105.91 for a single wallet (26,690 over 252), so <=121 bytes/row still holds — AT 40,000 ROWS THAT IS <=~4.84 MB AND ~97 CREDITS for a read that fills this ceiling, double what it was. The per-ROW headroom on resultBytesPerRowCeiling is 15.08 bytes and is UNAFFECTED by this raise: more rows buys a seventh column no room at all, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c still owns what one must do before it is added. WHAT THE RAISE COSTS THE CREDIT GUARD, priced rather than waved at: checkDuneAllowance converts the plan as maxExecutionsPerRun x worstCaseCreditsPerExecution + (maxExecutionsPerRun + 1) reads x this value x resultBytesPerRowCeiling at 20 credits/MB, so the worst case goes 2 x 25 + 3 x 20,000 x 121 B = 195.2 credits to 2 x 25 + 3 x 40,000 x 121 B = 340.4. At allowanceTightMultiple 2 and allowanceReserveCredits 25 a run now needs 705.8 of the period's 2,500 credits to read `sufficient` rather than `tight`, against 415.4 before — so a full-cap run still clears from a fresh period, and a period already ~72% spent warns where it used to pass. The guard still REFUSES before the first request and falls back to the RPC walk, which is the direction this leg fails in. A REAL RUN IS NOWHERE NEAR EITHER FIGURE: the three legs of 2026-08-05 read 2,937,602 / 200,869 / 282,958 result bytes, i.e. ~59 / ~4 / ~6 export credits. (2) THE ROWS BOUND, whose crossover moved WHILE THE SQL DID NOT: CREATION_SQL returns at most greatest(500, floor(19999 / <deployers in the batch>)) rows PER DEPLOYER — 500 a pinned floor, and 19,999 the value dune.mjs -> SQL_ROW_CEILING holds, both written as literals in the SQL because a saved Dune query cannot read this file, and both guarded by a test. So a run's rows are bounded at max(19,999, <deployers> x 500), which EXCEEDS THIS CEILING ABOVE 80 DEPLOYERS where it used to exceed it above 40 — and a result that does is still refused whole by the reader, exactly as before the cap existed, rather than published. It is NOT a by-construction bound and must not be quoted as one; the arithmetic a given run applies is visible in the dry run. SQL_ROW_CEILING IS DELIBERATELY LEFT AT 19,999 AND THE TWO ARE NO LONGER EQUAL. It used to be pinned at exactly this value minus one and DERIVED from it; the test now pins the INEQUALITY (SQL_ROW_CEILING <= maxResultRows - 1) instead. TWO REASONS, and the second is the operational one. (a) The equality was a DERIVATION, not the safety property. What matters is that a result honouring the derived half of the per-deployer cap can never sit ON its own `?limit=`, and 19,999 < 40,000 satisfies that more strongly than 19,999 < 20,000 did. What the frozen literal costs is that a ONE-wallet batch is still capped at 19,999 rows rather than 39,999 — which binds nothing: the largest per-wallet history this repo has measured is 247 and the industrial-spam extreme reachable from the total_bonded leaderboard is 8,518, both far under 19,999. Above 39 deployers the 500 floor binds and the share-out is not consulted at all, so the frozen literal is invisible on every batch a real run makes. (b) EDITING CREATION_SQL IS HALF A CHANGE: assertSavedQueryMatches compares the committed text against saved Dune query 8204672 BEFORE spending an execution, so a repo-side edit not deployed in place refuses the WHOLE Dune leg terminally, on every run, until they agree. Raising this ceiling by editing only this file needs no deploy and therefore cannot leave the leg refusing; re-coupling the two is a separate change that carries that deploy step and buys nothing measurable. See creationQueryId and README.md -> 'Deploying a change to the committed SQL'. WHY THE 500 FLOOR EXISTS AND WHY THIS RAISE DOES NOT TOUCH IT: a purely derived cap is 102 rows at the 195-candidate cap, which would truncate the subject deployer (247 launches, the reproduction control) and 4q4GKBpV (152) on every full run — a systematic per-wallet failure biased towards the largest and most gate-relevant wallets, which is worse than the rare all-or-nothing one it replaced. 500 is ~2x the largest per-wallet history this repo has measured (8/10/65/152/247, CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.3), so NO measured deployer is capped at any batch size, and ~17x below the industrial-spam extreme (8,518 deploys), so a spam wallet is still contained. It is pinned on its own evidence and moves only on its own. WHY THAT SECOND BOUND EXISTS AT ALL: this ceiling refuses the WHOLE RESULT, and enumeration is ONE execution for the whole batch, so before the cap a single industrial-spam deployer (README records an 8,518-deploy wallet reachable from the total_bonded leaderboard, one of the seeds) carried every other candidate past it and sent the entire run to the RPC walk — ~13 hours of walking traded against ~1 credit of Dune, decided by one outlier. The cap moves that refusal onto the wallet that earned it: a deployer whose true count exceeds its share is detected exactly (declared count above rows returned), refused with a reason, and walks alone. THE CEILING IS KEPT AS THE BACKSTOP rather than deleted, and it stays genuinely REACHABLE — preserving that is what the raise had to do rather than undo. Roughly 80 wallets of 500+ launches in one batch put a result past it, and at the shape actually measured (27,731 rows over 76 deployers = 364.9 rows/deployer) it is reached at about 109 deployers, both under the 195-candidate cap; such a run falls back whole exactly as merged main already did — never worse than today, just not eliminated. Under captain decision 262a's TIERED default the measured shape is far lighter — 1,896 rows over 69 deployers and 2,672 over 59, i.e. 27.5 and 45.3 rows a deployer — so a default run sits two orders of magnitude clear of this ceiling and the raise is insurance for a wide or untiered batch rather than a change to the normal case. Reaching it otherwise means the cap did not apply — a saved query edited past the committed text, or a shape the reader does not understand — and a soft bound on a billed read is not a bound. WHAT A REAL RUN COSTS AGAINST IT: at the 195-candidate cap and a median deployer history of ~50 launches, ~9,750 rows is ~0.95 MB, about 20 credits — roughly 125 full-cap runs a month, unchanged by this raise because a median-shaped batch never approaches either ceiling. The ceiling REFUSES rather than pages: an unbounded read is an unbounded bill, and a paged one would spend the allowance discovering how big the answer was.
justification.pollIntervalMs: 3,000 ms between status polls. MEASURED 2026-08-03: the two executions finished in 6 s and 9 s, so a run polls two or three times. Polling faster would buy at most a couple of seconds against a leg that replaces a walk measured in hours, and it is a shared free-tier host. Polling is a READ and costs no execution credit, but every poll counts against maxRequestsPerRun, which is what stops a slow execution turning into an unbounded loop.
justification.maxPollAttempts: 40 polls at 3,000 ms is 120 s, against the 6-9 s the two committed executions actually took — roughly 13x the observed worst. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE, and it is stated as an operational bound rather than dressed up: nothing in this repo measures the tail of Dune execution latency, because two executions is not a distribution. What would justify a value: execution durations over a month of scheduled runs, which the run record's dune block will accumulate. The failure direction is the safe one — running out of polls abandons the Dune leg and falls back to the RPC walk, and the execution is billed either way, so the cost of being wrong here is bounded by one execution.
justification.minIntervalMs: 250 ms between request starts, and NO MEASUREMENT OF THIS HOST BACKS IT. It is a courtesy floor on a free tier, carried across from creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200 ms, which WAS measured, on a different vendor) and rounded up rather than down. A real run issues about 8 requests, so the pacing costs ~2 s of a run measured in minutes and buying a measurement of it would be spending a shared allowance to tune something that is not a cost. What would justify a value: a pacing ladder against Dune's status endpoint recording shed events per rung, which is exactly what was done for Helius and has not been done here.
justification.maxCoverageLagMs: 6 hours. The probe cannot vouch for a period it does not reach, and the recent end is precisely where a live screen looks — a deployer that launched this morning is the one a discovery feed just surfaced. Dune's own freshness was measured by the scout at ~3-4 minutes (report.md section 6, item 8), so 6 hours is about 100x the vendor's lag and is not a tight bar; what it actually bounds is OUR cache, since the probe defaults to a cached read that could be arbitrarily old. THE FAILURE IS REPAIRED RATHER THAN INHERITED: when staleness is the ONLY thing wrong, dune.mjs re-executes the probe once, which is the second of the two budgeted executions. A structural refusal — a missing table, a month with no rows — is not retried, because asking the same question again returns the same answer.
justification.worstCaseCreditsPerExecution: 25 credits, the WORST case one of this leg's executions may cost, and it is the input the monthly-ceiling guard converts a plan into money with (client.mjs -> estimatePlanCredits). It has to be pinned per lane because DUNE PUBLISHES NO PRICE TABLE FOR EXECUTION COMPUTE — the evaluation lane recorded exactly that, and the cost depends entirely on what the statement scans. MEASURED on this account, 2026-08-03, for THESE two queries: the enumeration 0.919 execution credits and the coverage probe 0.751, and scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter (measured at 5 and at 20). The widest execution any slot-zero lane has recorded that does NOT join the trade tape is 19.25 credits (a curated-schema table listing, `slot-zero-launch-venue-daily-rates` section 7, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo); the two that DID join `dex_solana.trades` cost 81.74 and 221.51, which is why the figure is a per-lane pin and not a repository constant. 25 is ~27x the measured cost of the queries this leg actually runs and just above the widest non-trade-join execution on record. NEITHER QUERY MAY GROW A TRADE JOIN WITHOUT MOVING THIS NUMBER: CREATION_SQL and COVERAGE_SQL read the decoded create surfaces only, and a statement that reached the trade tape would be ~9x this pin with nothing else failing.
justification.resultBytesPerRowCeiling: 121 bytes per result row, UNCHANGED at SIX columns and, for the first time, backed by a measurement of the production shape rather than by arithmetic over an unobserved column. It is pinned here because the credit guard needs it as a number, and a bound that exists only in a sentence cannot be arithmetic. HISTORY: measured 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns, ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes); the fifth, launches_total, was then bounded by ARITHMETIC at <=24 bytes, and that is where 121 came from. CAPTAIN DECISION 227a ADDS A SIXTH, is_mayhem_mode, so this ceiling was RE-MEASURED rather than assumed to survive it — 2026-08-05, through enumerateCreations against the deployed query: 51,691 bytes over 488 rows in the same five-wallet batch shape = 105.92 bytes/row, and 26,690 bytes over 252 rows for ONE wallet = 105.91. Both sit under 121, so the pinned value DOES NOT MOVE. TWO THINGS THE RE-MEASUREMENT CHANGED THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE NUMBER. (1) The two shapes agree to two decimals, so total_result_set_bytes is per-row with negligible per-response overhead at these sizes — which CONTRADICTS the stated cause of the older ~115 bytes/row five-column reading (28,699 bytes over 250 rows, one wallet), which this file attributed to overhead amortised over fewer rows. A 252-row read now lands at the same figure as a 488-row one, so that explanation does not hold, the 115 does not reproduce in this accounting, and it must not be carried forward. (2) THE HEADROOM IS NOW THINNER THAN ONE MORE COLUMN IS WORTH: 121 - 105.92 = 15.08 bytes, against an arithmetic worst case of ~23 for a single boolean column (a JSON key plus `false`). So this ceiling survives the sixth column and would NOT survive a seventh by arithmetic. A SEVENTH COLUMN MUST RE-MEASURE AND RAISE THIS VALUE rather than lean on a margin that is no longer there. It bounds the EXPORT half of the worst case: maxResultRows x this x (maxExecutionsPerRun + 1) reads at 20 credits/MB. RAISING maxResultRows OR ADDING A COLUMN MOVES THIS, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c owns every figure above.
justification.allowanceReserveCredits: 25 credits held back from every allowance reading before the plan is compared against it, and it exists because THE COUNTER LAGS. Measured on this account during the Dune evaluation: `credits_used` rose +6.0 while the evaluator was completely idle, and it lands in whole-credit jumps — so a reading understates spend, therefore OVERSTATES what remains, and a guard that spent to the last credit would be spending money the vendor has already taken. It also absorbs part of a second gap it cannot measure: the key is SHARED, so another holder may spend between our reading and our execution. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE and it is stated rather than dressed up: 25 is ~4x the single observed drift and 1% of the free tier's 2,500. What would justify a value: a series of readings taken immediately before and after executions of known cost, which would price the lag distribution instead of one sample of it. The failure direction is the safe one — too large a reserve refuses a run that would have fitted, and this leg's refusal falls back to the RPC walk, which is slower rather than wrong.
justification.allowanceTightMultiple: 2. NOT A REFUSAL BAR — the threshold at which a run that WILL proceed prints a warning. A run whose worst case fits once but not twice may be the last one the period can afford, and an operator queueing heavier work behind it should learn that before the allowance is gone rather than from an HTTP 402 mid-run. NO MEASUREMENT BACKS THE 2, and here is what would: the distribution of Dune-spending runs per billing period, which does not exist because nothing here has yet run on a schedule. 2 is chosen as the smallest multiple that expresses 'this run is repeatable', which is the property that makes a failure recoverable.
justification.allowanceRequired: `true` — a run REFUSES the whole Dune leg when POST /usage cannot be read, rather than proceeding blind. NOT A MEASUREMENT, a policy, and it is the one the whole guard turns on: an unreadable balance is not headroom, and 'we could not see it' is the same evidence as 'it is empty'. The cost of being wrong is bounded and known — this leg falls back to the Solana RPC walk, which needs no Dune credential and is slower rather than wrong — while the cost of being wrong the other way is a billed multi-execution run that dies partway with neither a result nor the credits to retry. The reading itself is free (Dune documents /usage as a metadata endpoint consuming no credits) and is retried once, so a single transport hiccup does not reach this switch.
justification.refreshProbeByDefault: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch, and it is `false` because the probe is PARAMETERLESS and therefore has a cached answer that costs no execution at all. Re-executing it every run would spend the binding budget on a figure that moves by one row per second. `--dune-refresh-probe` makes it explicit, and staleness re-executes it anyway (see maxCoverageLagMs), so the default cannot silently publish a count over coverage nobody checked.

$comment: The SAME measurement as creation_walk, over an indexed provider instead of a raw signature
scan. It is used when HELIUS_API_KEY is set; with the key unset the creation_walk block above
governs and the run is byte-for-byte what it was before this block existed.
Helius getTransactionsForAddress applies `status: succeeded` server-side and returns the
transaction bodies in the same call, so it collapses BOTH halves of the keyless walk — page
signatures, then one getTransaction per survivor — into one request per 1,000 transactions.
PLAN: Helius Developer, $49/month, 10,000,000 credits/month, 50 requests/second (their
pricing page, read 2026-08-03). getTransactionsForAddress in `full` mode bills 10 CREDITS PER
100 TRANSACTIONS RETURNED, rounded up, 10 minimum; getMultipleAccounts is a standard method at
1 credit. The key is UNSHARED — it belongs to this research lane alone (captain, 2026-08-03),
so the whole allowance is this tool's and no other consumer can be starved by a heavy run.
CREDITS ARE THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, NOT WALL CLOCK, and that is the inversion this block
exists to record. The keyless walk was bounded by time: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s
is 13.5 hours. Here the same 195 candidates at the worst measured per-candidate cost is about
46 minutes — and 1,014,000 credits, which is 10.14% of a month's allowance in one run. DO NOT
'CORRECT' THAT 46 DOWN TO THE 32.5 THE PACING FLOOR IMPLIES: 195 x 50 pages x 200ms is the
naive arithmetic, and this walk is LATENCY-BOUND below ~250ms of enforced interval. The
2026-08-03 full-mode ladder (20 requests a rung, one in flight) measured 962/490/301/251/257 ms
per request at enforced intervals of 1000/500/250/100/0 ms, i.e. a floor of ~250-260ms set by
response latency (p50 ~220ms) with ~50ms of overhead once the interval dominates. At the pinned
200ms a page really costs ~280ms, so 195 x 50 x 280ms = 45.5 min. render.mjs prints the same
figure from MEASURED_PAGE_CYCLE_MS rather than from the interval. So the
ceiling below is stated in credits, and the page count is a SEPARATE bound rather than the
same one restated: since the per-page guard reserves the curve-classification pass on top of
a whole page, the credit ceiling carries headroom the page cap does not, and the page cap is
what binds first. See the two justifications for the arithmetic.

justification.maxCreditsPerCandidate: MEASURED 2026-08-03 against the only population where both readings exist: the twelve wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json, every one of them enumerated to EXHAUSTION. Succeeded-transaction counts per wallet: 168, 211, 1007, 1026, 2136, 2989, 3344, 4749, 6378, 7791, 46815, 49367 — median ~3,167, max 49,367. At 10 credits per 100 returned that is 20, 30, 110, 110, 220, 300, 340, 480, 640, 780, 4690, 4940 credits for a COMPLETE history, median ~320, max 4,940, and 12,660 for all twelve together. THE CEILING IS 5,200 RATHER THAN 5,000 BECAUSE THE PER-PAGE GUARD COSTS MORE THAN A PAGE, and the arithmetic has to be stated or the next reader re-derives 5,000 and reintroduces the defect: a page is only STARTED when a whole page's worst case still fits ALONGSIDE the curve-classification reservation, and that reservation is creditsForCurveReads(creates.length + pageLimit) = ceil(n/100) + 1, whose floor at pageLimit 1,000 is 11. So the guard demands 100 + 11 = 111 credits free, not 100. At 5,000 the walk could start a page only while 111 remained, which after 49 full pages leaves 100 and stops on `credit-ceiling` at 49,000 transactions — SHORT OF THE 49,367 OF 6Wg4aeZ2, the very wallet the ceiling was sized against, so the population's largest history would have truncated while this text claimed it did not. 5,200 affords 51 data pages, past both the 50-page cap and that largest history, so every wallet in the measured population walks its whole index rather than a window — which is the coverage this route buys and the reason the ceiling is not set at the median. The reservation itself is not negotiable: CREATION-DERIVED.md §4 owns it, and a walk that spends its last unit finding one more creation has bought a launch it must then score as NOT bonded, deflating the very rate the walk was widening. The failure direction is the one the keyless walk already has and already reports: a wallet costlier than 5,200 credits stops on `credit-ceiling`, its covered window is a window and says so, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing beyond it. WHAT WOULD MOVE IT: a wallet measured above 49,367 succeeded transactions whose reading the gate needs whole, or a change to pageLimit or to creditsForCurveReads, both of which move the 111.
justification.maxCreditsPerRun: 11% of the Developer plan's 10,000,000 monthly credits, chosen so that the DEFAULT plan is admissible and the arithmetic is visible: maxCandidates 195 x maxCreditsPerCandidate 5,200 = 1,014,000 worst case, which fits under 1,100,000 with margin. THE TWO CEILINGS ARE COUPLED AND MUST MOVE TOGETHER — that is the whole reason this one changed: screen.mjs refuses a plan whose worst case exceeds this value BEFORE its first request, so raising the per-candidate ceiling from 5,000 to 5,200 while leaving this at 1,000,000 would have made EVERY default run refuse to start (1,014,000 > 1,000,000). That worst case is ~10.14% of the monthly allowance, so roughly nine worst-case full-cap runs fit in a month, and the measured EXPECTED cost is far lower — at the median per-candidate 320 credits a full 195-candidate run is about 62,400 credits, i.e. 0.62% of the month, so roughly 160 such runs would fit. THE POINT IS THE REFUSAL, NOT THE NUMBER: screen.mjs computes the worst case before its first request and refuses a plan that does not fit, so raising either per-candidate bound or the candidate cap without raising this one stops the run BEFORE it spends rather than part-way through, which is the same rule the keyed and keyless ceilings already enforce. NOTHING HERE TRACKS THE MONTH: this tool holds no state between runs and cannot see what the allowance has already paid for, so this bounds ONE run and the monthly arithmetic is the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxPagesPerCandidate: NOT the same bound as maxCreditsPerCandidate any more, and the correction is the point: it USED to be an exact restatement — a full page of pageLimit 1,000 costs exactly 100 credits, so 5,000 credits was precisely 50 pages and neither could bind before the other. That stopped being true when the credit ceiling rose to 5,200 to clear the 111-credit per-page guard (see maxCreditsPerCandidate). At 5,200 the credit ceiling affords 51 data pages, so THE PAGE CAP IS NOW WHAT BINDS FIRST and the credit ceiling carries the guard's headroom behind it. 50 is kept rather than raised because 50 pages is 50,000 transactions, still above the largest history measured (49,367), so the measured population still walks whole; and the page cap exists at all because the walk's loop counts pages, and because a future pageLimit change would otherwise silently move the page bound with no line saying so.
justification.pageLimit: 1000 is the endpoint's own maximum and it is enforced rather than documented-only: `limit: 5000` returns HTTP 200 carrying {"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"Bad request: Invalid limit: You can only request up to 1000 transactions at a time…"}} (measured 2026-08-03). Asking for less would multiply both the request count and the 10-credit-per-page MINIMUM — a walk at limit 100 pays the same 10 credits for a tenth of the answer — so the endpoint's cap is also the cheapest setting.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, stated as one, exactly like creation_walk.maxTransactionsPerCandidate. 50 pages x 1,000 = 50,000, so this equals the page bound and no walk can reach it first. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising maxPagesPerCandidate or pageLimit does not silently remove the only bound expressed in the unit the parser actually works in. No measurement fixes it beyond the page arithmetic above, and inventing one would be worse than saying so.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this endpoint, this plan, this client shape (one request in flight). A pacing ladder over getTransactionsForAddress against the busiest measured wallet — full mode at 1000/500/250/100/0 ms, 20 requests a rung, and signatures mode at 500/200/100/50/0 ms, 30 a rung — recorded ZERO shed events and zero JSON-RPC errors at EVERY rung, including 0 ms. Throughput saturated well below the plan's documented 50 req/s because the walk is latency-bound, not limit-bound: full pages returned p50 ~220 ms and topped out at 3.98 req/s (interval 100) against 3.89 (interval 0), signature pages at 7.54 against 7.38. A separate concurrency probe of 150 simultaneous requests observed 161 req/s with all 150 answered 200, so the documented ceiling was never reached at any pacing this client can produce serially. 200 ms is therefore NOT a shed-avoidance figure — nothing shed — it is a courtesy floor with an order of magnitude of headroom under the documented 50 req/s, and it costs about 17% of wall clock against the fastest rung on a leg that now takes seconds. THIS IS THE FREE ENDPOINT'S OPPOSITE and the contrast is the point: creation_walk.rpcMinIntervalMs is 2,500 ms because api.mainnet-beta sheds a quarter of what it is asked for and the nominally faster 1,400 ms measured SLOWER once backoff was counted. BATCHING IS NOT USED AND WAS NOT RE-MEASURED, because it no longer applies: this route issues one request per 1,000 transactions instead of one per transaction, so there is nothing left to batch. The JSON-RPC batching finding recorded against api.mainnet-beta (58s at batch=1 with zero shed, 110s at batch=8 with eleven) is untouched and still governs the keyless fallback.

justification.maxKeyedRequests: 402 = 2 x (6 enumeration + 195 candidates), the ONE-RETRY WORST CASE OF THE PLAN — captain decision 267a, 2026-08-05. IT IS NO LONGER AN ALLOWANCE FIGURE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE CHANGE: it was 200, the entire Free-tier day, and the day is now 100,000 and EXCLUSIVE to slot-zero (x-ratelimit-limit read off the wire 2026-08-05, see this block's $comment). An allowance-derived per-run ceiling would now sit four orders of magnitude above any plan and refuse nothing, and this file's standing rule is that a bound which cannot refuse is not a bound. So the value is derived from what a run can actually ISSUE instead. THE ARITHMETIC: enumeration costs 6 requests, not 3, since captain decision 262a made the seeding TIERED by default (seed.mjs -> DEFAULT_TIERS, one pass of recent-bonds/alerts/leaderboard per tier for `good` and `elite`), and the gate costs 1 per candidate, so a plan at the 195-candidate cap DECLARES 201 (screen.mjs -> worstCaseKeyed, which counts first attempts). THE FACTOR OF 2 IS THE RETRY RULE MADE EXPLICIT: a keyed request is retried at most once on a 429/5xx/transport failure and EVERY ATTEMPT counts against this ceiling (client.mjs, maxRetriesPerRequest default 1), so 402 is the most requests a plan the tool ADMITTED can actually issue, and this ceiling can therefore never stop a run it already agreed to start. THE OLD 2-REQUEST HEADROOM COULD NOT PROMISE THAT: at 200 against a 198-request worst case, three transport failures near the end of a full run breached it, and the 2 was never a statement about retries — it was simply what the allowance left. NOTE THE FORCED HALF, so this does not read as an optional widening: at the old 200 a default plan now costs 6 + 195 = 201 and would be REFUSED BEFORE ITS FIRST REQUEST, so this value had to move the moment the seeding became tiered. A run whose PLANNED worst case exceeds this is still refused before its first request rather than allowed to die part-way through. STAGE 2 ADDS NOTHING TO THIS: it reuses the profile Stage 1 already fetched and spends no keyed request of its own. WHAT ONE RUN NOW COSTS THE DAY: 201 of 100,000 is 0.201%, or 0.402% at this ceiling — roughly 248 full-cap runs a day. Nothing here tracks the day across runs, so that arithmetic stays the operator's.
justification.maxCandidates: 195, UNCHANGED IN VALUE AND COMPLETELY RE-DERIVED — captain decision 267a, 2026-08-05. SAY THE COINCIDENCE OUT LOUD, because a reader seeing the same integer will assume nothing moved: it WAS `200 - 3 enumeration - 2 retry headroom`, i.e. what the MadeOnSol day left over, and that derivation is now void — the day is 100,000 and exclusive, which would license a cap of tens of thousands and mean nothing. Two different arithmetics landing on 195 is a coincidence of integers, not continuity, and the old sentence must not be quoted for it. THE VALUE IS NOW THE LARGEST CAP THAT FITS THE CEILINGS ALREADY PINNED WITHOUT MOVING A SECOND THRESHOLD, which is the principle stage2_entry.justification.maxCandidatesScored derives 7 from. Three bounds apply and the tightest wins. (1) THE KEYLESS FRONTEND-API-V3 CEILING, WHICH BINDS: maxKeylessRequests is 1,400 with 35 of retry headroom, and a candidate costs up to 4 gate listing pages plus 3 --consistency pages = 7, so floor(1,365 / 7) = 195 EXACTLY. Above it a --consistency plan is refused before its first request. (2) THE HELIUS RUN CEILING: creation_walk_helius.maxCreditsPerRun 1,100,000 / maxCreditsPerCandidate 5,200 = 211.5, so 211. (3) ENUMERATION REACH: 6 queries x 50 rows = 300 rows, the most distinct wallets one plan can hand the gate at all — screen.mjs caps the page limit at 50 and seed.mjs clamps alerts to the same 50, so the vendor's 100-row alerts ceiling is never asked for (an earlier version of this entry read 50 + 100 + 50 over three queries, which overstated the reach). 195 is the minimum of the three, so RAISING IT CASCADES into two pinned ceilings, with the keyless RPC wall clock behind them — which is why 267a did not raise it, and why 'the day got 500x bigger' is not on its own a reason to. IT STILL COVERS WHAT ENUMERATION ACTUALLY SURFACES, which is the property this cap exists for: the highest distinct yield ever observed is 128 (2026-08-05, good 69 + elite 59, the two tier pools DISJOINT that day — runs/2026-08-05-seed-comparison.md), against 22 elite-only on 2026-07-29, 72 good-only on 2026-08-02 and 76 untiered on 2026-08-05. So the cap sits ~52% above the observed maximum, the DEFAULT run grades everything it surfaces, and coverage truncation stays the exception it is supposed to be. THE HEADROOM IS NOT PERMANENT: tier pools grow — the elite pool was 2.7x its 2026-07-29 size by 2026-08-05 — so a run record showing candidates AT the cap is evidence this needs re-deriving, not evidence of a busy day.
justification.keyedMinIntervalMs: 250ms, RE-MEASURED ON ULTRA RATHER THAN CARRIED ACROSS — captain decision 267a required exactly that, and the measurement RETIRED the constraint the old value existed for. IT WAS 6,500ms, justified on the vendor enforcing a ~10/minute burst limit: 'the vendor's rate limit, not our caution', which is precisely the kind of claim that has to be re-checked when the tier changes rather than inherited. MEASURED 2026-08-05 against the live Ultra key, one request in flight, on the two endpoints a run actually spends on. A pacing ladder over /deployer-hunter/leaderboard at enforced intervals of 6,500 / 2,000 / 500 / 0 ms, 12 requests a rung, recorded ZERO shed events and zero non-200 responses at EVERY RUNG INCLUDING 0 ms; then 60 back-to-back requests at 0 ms — 19.7 s, 3.05 req/s, i.e. ~183/minute sustained — also shed NOTHING, which a ~10/minute limiter would have refused at request 11. The gate's own endpoint, /deployer-hunter/{wallet}, behaved the same: 30 back-to-back, 0 shed, 4.95 req/s, and x-ratelimit-used advanced by exactly 30, so the counter is per-request and global across endpoints rather than per-endpoint. So the ~10/minute figure does not describe this tier and 6,500ms was buying nothing. WHAT BINDS INSTEAD IS RESPONSE LATENCY, exactly as on Helius: p50 312ms on the leaderboard and 182ms on the profile endpoint, so one serial client tops out near 3-5 req/s whatever the interval says. 250ms is therefore A COURTESY FLOOR AND NOT A SHED-AVOIDANCE FIGURE — the same character as creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200ms, measured the same way on a vendor that also shed nothing) and the same number this file already pins for its other keyed host in dune.minIntervalMs. It sits at or below the measured latency of both endpoints, so it costs a run essentially nothing while keeping a serial floor in place rather than none at all. THREE LIMITS ON THAT MEASUREMENT, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: it is ONE DAY, on ~150 requests, so it bounds nothing about a sustained multi-hour leg; it says nothing about CONCURRENCY, because this client issues one request at a time and no probe put several in flight; and it cannot see a limiter that only bites well above 183/minute, which serial pacing structurally cannot reach. What would extend it: a rung ladder repeated across several days, and a concurrency probe of the shape creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs records. The 'margin matters because the allowance is shared' half of the old reasoning is void rather than merely weakened — the key is EXCLUSIVE since captain, 2026-08-05. THE WALL-CLOCK CONSEQUENCE IS LARGE AND IS WHAT A READER WANTS FIRST: the keyed leg of a full 201-request run goes from ABOUT 21 MINUTES to ABOUT 50 SECONDS. THAT WAS NEVER THE RUN'S WALL CLOCK AND STILL IS NOT. The default history source is creation-derived, and the Solana RPC walk dominates everything else by an order of magnitude: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s is ~13.5 HOURS on its own. Add ~50 seconds keyed, ~26 minutes for the gate's ownership listing on frontend-api-v3, ~147 for Stage 2 on swap-api (7 x 10 x 18), up to ~146 more for Stage 2's cost leg (stage2_cost, 7 x 500 requests at the same 2.5s, and it SHARES this limiter rather than adding a second queue), and a further ~19.5 with --consistency, and a full default run at the candidate cap is ABOUT 18.9 HOURS end to end, or ~19.2 with --consistency. Those two Stage 2 legs multiplied when the scoring cap went 3 -> 7 on 2026-08-04; stage2_entry.justification.maxCandidatesScored owns that raise and its cost, and this entry only carries the total. Earlier versions of this note said 47 minutes (it predated the creation walk and was wrong by a factor of twenty) and then 19.2 hours (correct while keyed pacing was 6.5s, which contributed ~21 minutes of it). DO NOT KILL A DEFAULT RUN FOR STILL GOING AFTER AN HOUR. The liveness signal is not the same on every leg: the keyed and frontend-api-v3 clients print one line per request, but the creation walk would emit ~20,000 of those, so it prints a PERIODIC HEARTBEAT — the first request of each candidate and then every tenth, i.e. a line roughly every 25 seconds at this walk's 2.5s pacing, showing that candidate's spend against maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate. Watch that counter rather than expecting a line per request, and use --candidates N to bound the run (the RPC leg is N x 100 x 2.5s) or --ownership-only to skip the walk entirely for a fast pass whose bias runs BOTH ways at once — it REJECTS through the count bars and INFLATES through the rate — and is stamped into the record as historySource: 'ownership-only'. renderDryRun prints this arithmetic for whatever flags are actually passed.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: frontend-api-v3.pump.fun — the gate's ownership listing and the --consistency creator walk, which share one client. It does NOT govern the Stage 2 fill walk, which has its own pinned pacing (`stage2_entry.keylessMinIntervalMs`) because it reaches a different host that behaves differently. THIS VALUE IS A CONSERVATIVE CARRY-OVER, NOT A MEASUREMENT OF THE ENDPOINT IT GOVERNS, and the correction matters: the ~0.5 requests/second figure this was originally justified by was measured against api.mainnet-beta.solana.com, and the June report's own spend table records BOTH swap-api.pump.fun and frontend-api-v3.pump.fun as NOT CONTACTED — so it was never a pump.fun measurement at all. It is kept because it is conservative and because frontend-api-v3 has shed nothing in this tool's use of it; if that host is ever measured, this number should be re-derived from that measurement rather than from a different host's. Either way it bounds a shared public resource rather than expressing our own caution, so the MadeOnSol relaxation does not touch it. The RETRY COUNT is a separate question and is not this bound: a keyless request is retried on a 429 or a 5xx, and each attempt counts against maxKeylessRequests.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: A PER-CLIENT CEILING, NOT A RUN TOTAL, and the distinction is what the code enforces: screen.mjs builds TWO independent keyless clients, and this value bounds only the general one (frontend-api-v3). Stage 2 runs on its own client under its own `stage2_entry.maxKeylessRequests` of 1,260, which this number neither contains nor constrains, so the enforced combined worst case is 1,400 + 1,260 = 2,660 requests (it was 1,400 + 540 = 1,940 before the proof-coverage lane raised the scoring cap to 7 on 2026-08-04, and 1,400 + 432 = 1,832 before captain decision 190a raised the launch cap to 10). 1,400 is sized to COVER the candidate cap rather than to bound it, and it is sized for what the code now actually spends on this client, which is TWO passes and not one. The GATE reads the ownership listing it merges the creation window with, up to 4 pages PER CANDIDATE (screen.mjs LISTING_PAGES_FOR_MERGE); the --consistency pass then costs up to 3 pages per gate SURVIVOR, and every candidate can be one. So 195 candidates cost 195 x 4 = 780 for the gate plus 195 x 3 = 585 for consistency = 1,365 worst case, and the remaining 35 are the retry headroom. The earlier 600 was justified on the consistency pass alone and was already exceeded by gating at the default candidate cap. SINCE CAPTAIN DECISION 267a THIS ENTRY ALSO FIXES maxCandidates, AND THE DEPENDENCY NOW RUNS THE OTHER WAY: 1,365 / 7 pages a candidate = 195 EXACTLY, which is the tightest of the three bounds on the candidate cap and therefore the one that sets it. Before 267a the keyed allowance set the cap and this ceiling was sized to COVER it; the MadeOnSol day is now 100,000 and exclusive and binds nothing, so the two swapped roles without either number moving. justification.maxEntryCostPerSolStaked: PINNED ON MEASUREMENT, and the measurement is the create-slot half of the same reproduction. Entry cost is a wallet's real lamport outflow in its create-slot transaction less the swap-quote SOL it committed there, so it is the fee (base and priority), the venue fee, the rent, the execution difference and any tip paid inside that transaction. THE UNIT THIS BAR IS COMPARED AGAINST IS THE PER-LAUNCH MEDIAN, not the pooled per-entry one (captain decision 140a): every scored launch contributes its own median entry and exactly one observation, so a launch with dozens of priced entrants cannot outvote a launch with one. entry.mjs computes both — entryCostPerSolStakedByLaunch is what the verdict reads, entryCostPerSolStaked is the finer-grained per-entry evidence reported beside it — and a test pins the gate to the per-launch unit. THE DENOMINATOR IS THE SEAT, NOT THE WHOLE STAKE, and the name understates that: the per-entry ratio is entryCostSol / FieldEntrant.createSlotFillSol — the entrant's own create-slot curve buy — and NOT its whole-window FieldEntrant.stakeSol. On the committed tape the two coincide for the median entrant (stakeSol / createSlotFillSol reads p50 1.000, p90 1.000, max 47.63 over 757 priced entries), and the seat is the smaller denominator, so the implemented ratio is the LARGER one and this bar is the easier one to trip — conservative, which is the direction the cost leg must fail in. Re-derived 2026-08-02 from the same population Stage 0's verifyOnChainCostReproduction prices, which since 2026-08-02 is the GATED one — proven create-slot openings only, matching what scoreEntry itself scores (data/population-tape-2026-07-29/onchain_create_slot_pnl.csv, 110 launches, 757 create-slot entries): the PER-LAUNCH median is 0.0389 SOL per SOL staked, p90 0.0985, and the WORST LAUNCH ON THE TAPE IS 0.3311; pooled over the 757 individual entries the median is 0.0369, p75 0.0812, p90 0.1970. Post-break alone (78 launches, 492 entries): per-launch median 0.0354, p90 0.0571, worst launch 0.1361; per-entry median 0.0292. Leaving the unproven openings in — the population this check used to price — reads 113 / 775 and a per-launch median of 0.0388, i.e. 0.0001 CHEAPER, which is why the gated figure is the one quoted. The bar is 0.12, and what fixes it there is the field's own gross return over that same gated population: the median closed round trip returned 0.1246 SOL per SOL staked gross (460 pairs — the same 460 minFieldHitRateGross names below). A seat priced at 0.12 therefore costs essentially the whole of the gross prize, and since gross is an upper bound the median entrant cannot clear it — that is arithmetic, not a preference. The bar sits inside the observed range rather than above it, so it is not decorative: the worst-priced launch this project has ever measured would trip it. NOTE THE DIRECTION OF THE ERROR: an out-of-transaction landing tip is NOT in the numerator, so the measured price of the seat is a LOWER bound and this bar is harder to trip than the truth warrants. That is the optimistic direction, which is why the cost leg is a gate and never a pass.
justification.minPricedFraction: 0.8 of the create-slot field must be priced on-chain before any after-cost reading may stand. This is the coverage floor behind rule 1 of the ruling — unmeasured cost is never a pass — and the failure it exists for is specific: the cost walk goes launch by launch under a per-candidate RPC ceiling, so a budget that runs out part-way leaves a cost distribution describing only the launches walked FIRST, which are the newest ones. That is a biased sample rather than a short one, and a biased sample of a cost is a wrong number. 0.8 bounds the unpriced share to a fifth. THE CEILING COSTS WHOLE LAUNCHES AND NEVER HALF OF ONE, and that is enforced at BOTH ends rather than asserted: a launch is not started unless the remaining budget covers its whole target list, and — because that reservation cannot see retries or a re-asked null getTransaction, so the ceiling can still bite mid-walk — a launch that came back short is DISCARDED whole, its partial pricing dropped and the launch counted in entry.coverage.cost.launchesDiscarded (entry.coverage.cost.launchesSkippedForBudget is the other end: launches the reservation never started, on which nothing was spent). Without the second half the bias this bar exists to bound would reappear one level down, inside a launch, where a truncated walk holds the earliest entrants by slot. It is a floor on OUR coverage and not a property of any deployer, so falling below it yields entry-cost-unmeasured — an absence of a finding, never a finding of absence.
justification.minFieldHitRateGross: A NECESSARY CONDITION, NEVER A SUFFICIENT ONE, and it can only ever take a verdict away. The fill tape is gross of fees, so this rate is an upper bound: on our own subject's post-2026-06-04 launches the screen now reads 0.763 (351 of 460 closed round trips positive, over the 86 launches whose opening is proven; the superseded reading was 0.765 over 473, taken before unproven openings stopped being scored) while the fee-inclusive record puts the whole outsider population at +0.54 SOL per launch with 51 of 106 wallets negative. Below 0.5 the field loses money before costs and therefore certainly after them, which is conclusive; above it, nothing whatsoever is established. Stage 0 asserts that this leg cannot carry a positive verdict on its own.
